items.stem: Foreign direct investment is
options: investment by a firm in productive assets in another country, with a lasting management interest
aid given by a foreign government
items.answer: investment by a firm in productive assets in another country, with a lasting management interest
items.markingKey: E.g. building a factory abroad; differs from portfolio investment.

items.stem: Explain two possible disadvantages of FDI for a developing country.
items.answer: Repatriation of profits; transfer pricing and tax avoidance; crowding out of domestic firms; environmental damage; low-skilled jobs only; political influence; footloose firms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why multinational companies invest in developing countries.
items.answer: Lower labour and land costs; access to raw materials and new markets; to avoid trade barriers; tax incentives; economies of scale.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason [2]

items.stem: A multinational in Quentara makes a profit of $40 million and pays 30% tax there. It sends 50% of after-tax profit home. Calculate the profit repatriated.
items.answer: $14 million

items.stem: A multinational invests $500 million in Pelora, employing 2,000 local workers at $6,000 a year. Annual profit is $80 million, taxed at 30%, and 80% of after-tax profit is repatriated. (a) Calculate tax paid, the local wage bill and profit repatriated. (b) If transfer pricing moved 20% of the profit to a zero-tax country, calculate the tax lost to Pelora. (c) Assess whether the FDI benefits Pelora.
items.answer: (a) Tax $24m; wages $12m; repatriated $44.8m (b) $4.8m (c) Benefits: jobs, wages, tax, technology, exports; costs: repatriation, transfer pricing, environmental or competition effects; net benefit depends on linkages and regulation.
items.markingKey: (a) three calculations [3]; (b) shifted profit × tax rate [1]; (c) balanced assessment [2].

items.stem: A multinational invests $800 million in Korvia, employing 1,500 local workers at $4,000 a year. Annual profit is $40 million, taxed at 20%, and 60% of after-tax profit is repatriated. (a) Calculate tax paid, the local wage bill and profit repatriated. (b) If transfer pricing moved 30% of the profit to a zero-tax country, calculate the tax lost to Korvia. (c) Assess whether the FDI benefits Korvia.
items.answer: (a) Tax $8m; wages $6m; repatriated $19.2m (b) $2.4m (c) Benefits: jobs, wages, tax, technology, exports; costs: repatriation, transfer pricing, environmental or competition effects; net benefit depends on linkages and regulation.
items.markingKey: (a) three calculations [3]; (b) shifted profit × tax rate [1]; (c) balanced assessment [2].

items.stem: Extract: Umbria Nova relies on copper for 70% of its exports. Over five years its export price index fell to 82 while its import price index rose to 110. External debt has reached 90% of GDP and the government is negotiating an IMF loan, while a foreign mining company plans a new mine. (a) Explain two conditions the IMF might attach to its loan. (b) Explain one way the country could reduce its dependence on copper.
items.answer: (a) Fiscal consolidation, removal of subsidies, exchange-rate flexibility, privatisation, anti-corruption measures. (b) Diversification into processing/manufacturing or services; sovereign wealth fund.

items.stem: Extract: Esteria relies on copper for 70% of its exports. Over five years its export price index fell to 82 while its import price index rose to 110. External debt has reached 75% of GDP and the government is negotiating an IMF loan, while a foreign mining company plans a new mine. (a) Calculate the change in the terms of trade. (b) Explain how the change in the terms of trade may have contributed to the debt problem.
items.answer: (a) ToT = 82/110 × 100 = 74.5: a deterioration of 25.5% (b) Lower export earnings relative to imports widen the current account deficit, financed by borrowing.

items.stem: Transfer pricing by a multinational company involves
options: setting internal prices between its subsidiaries to shift profits to low-tax countries
setting the same price in all countries
items.answer: setting internal prices between its subsidiaries to shift profits to low-tax countries
items.markingKey: Reduces tax paid in high-tax host countries.

items.stem: A multinational in Merania makes a profit of $80 million and pays 20% tax there. It sends 75% of after-tax profit home. Calculate the profit repatriated.
items.answer: $48 million

items.stem: Granite Holdings, a global company, has announced a $2 billion investment in Lunaria. Consider whether foreign direct investment by multinational companies always benefits developing countries.
items.answer: Arguments for: Jobs, capital, technology, tax, exports. Arguments against / evaluation: Repatriation, transfer pricing, environmental damage, crowding out, footloose; depends on regulation and linkages. Conclusion: a supported judgement that depends on the conditions identified.
items.markingKey: Knowledge and analysis (about 60%): accurate theory, logical chains of reasoning and a relevant diagram described with axes, curves and shifts. Evaluation (about 40%): considers both sides, the assumptions and the context, and reaches a justified conclusion.

items.stem: Tied aid is aid that
options: must be spent on goods and services from the donor country
items.answer: must be spent on goods and services from the donor country
items.markingKey: Reduces value to recipient; benefits donor exporters.

items.stem: Explain two reasons why foreign aid may not promote development.
items.answer: Corruption and misuse; tied aid reduces value; aid dependency; crowding out of local producers (food aid); spending on prestige projects; conditions that harm the poor.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain how aid can help to close the savings gap in a developing country.
items.answer: Low incomes mean low saving and investment (Harrod–Domar); aid supplements domestic saving to fund investment in capital and infrastructure, raising growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: savings gap; 1 mark: aid funds investment/growth [2]

items.stem: Esteria has GNI of $1,500 billion and gives $9 billion in official development assistance. Calculate aid as a percentage of GNI.

Nordavia has GNI of $500 billion and gives $14 billion in aid. 40% of its aid is tied, and tied goods cost 20% more than on the world market. (a) Calculate aid as a % of GNI and the extra aid needed to meet the 0.7% target. (b) Calculate the loss in value to recipients from tying. (c) Explain one other drawback of tied aid.
items.answer: (a) 2.8%; extra needed $0 billion (b) $1.12 billion (c) Recipients cannot choose suitable or cheapest goods; may not match needs; benefits donor firms; may create dependency on donor parts and services.
items.markingKey: (a) share [1]; 0.7% × GNI − aid [1]; (b) tied aid × premium [2]; (c) drawback [1].

items.stem: Extract: Korvia relies on copper for 70% of its exports. Over five years its export price index fell to 82 while its import price index rose to 110. (a) Explain how the change in the terms of trade may have contributed to the debt problem. (b) Explain one way the country could reduce its dependence on copper.
items.answer: (a) Lower export earnings relative to imports widen the current account deficit, financed by borrowing. (b) Diversification into processing/manufacturing or services; sovereign wealth fund.

items.stem: Food aid is shipped free to Pelora after a good harvest. Explain how this could harm local farmers.
items.answer: Free food increases supply and lowers local prices, reducing farmers’ incomes and incentives to produce, and may create dependency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price fall; 1 mark: incomes/incentives [2]

items.stem: Westaria has GNI of $1,500 billion and gives $3 billion in aid. 40% of its aid is tied, and tied goods cost 25% more than on the world market. (a) Calculate aid as a % of GNI and the extra aid needed to meet the 0.7% target. (b) Calculate the loss in value to recipients from tying. (c) Explain one other drawback of tied aid.
items.answer: (a) 0.2%; extra needed $7.5 billion (b) $0.3 billion (c) Recipients cannot choose suitable or cheapest goods; may not match needs; benefits donor firms; may create dependency on donor parts and services.
items.markingKey: (a) share [1]; 0.7% × GNI − aid [1]; (b) tied aid × premium [2]; (c) drawback [1].

items.stem: The debt service ratio is
options: debt service payments as a percentage of export earnings
items.answer: debt service payments as a percentage of export earnings
items.markingKey: Shows ability to service external debt from exports.

items.stem: Explain two causes of high external debt in developing countries.
items.answer: Persistent current account deficits; borrowing for projects that did not generate returns; rising world interest rates; currency depreciation; falling commodity prices reducing export earnings.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: Explain why IMF conditions attached to loans are controversial.
items.answer: Austerity and structural adjustment may cut public services and raise unemployment and poverty in the short run, though they aim to restore stability and growth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: conditions; 1 mark: social cost vs stability [2]

items.stem: Westaria has external debt of $30 billion and GDP of $80 billion. Calculate the debt-to-GDP ratio.

Quentara has external debt of $60 billion in dollars at an interest rate of 6%, and repays $2 billion of principal each year. Export earnings are $20 billion and GDP is $50 billion. (a) Calculate annual debt service and the debt service ratio. (b) The currency depreciates by 25% against the dollar. Explain the effect on the burden of the debt.
items.answer: (a) Debt service = 3.6 + 2 = $5.6 billion; DSR = 28% of exports. (b) The dollar debt is unchanged but costs more local currency (each dollar needs more units); if export prices are in dollars the DSR is unchanged, but the burden on the government budget and local firms rises.
items.markingKey: (a) interest + principal [1]; ÷ exports [1]; (b) depreciation raises local-currency cost [2].

items.stem: Extract: Merania relies on copper for 70% of its exports. Over five years its export price index fell to 78 while its import price index rose to 104. External debt has reached 75% of GDP and the government is negotiating an IMF loan, while a foreign mining company plans a new mine. (a) Explain two conditions the IMF might attach to its loan. (b) Explain one way the country could reduce its dependence on copper.
items.answer: (a) Fiscal consolidation, removal of subsidies, exchange-rate flexibility, privatisation, anti-corruption measures. (b) Diversification into processing/manufacturing or services; sovereign wealth fund.

items.stem: World interest rates rise sharply. Explain the effect on a developing country such as Rovania with large variable-rate external debts.
items.answer: Interest payments rise, increasing debt service and the debt service ratio, diverting foreign exchange and budget revenue from development spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: higher interest cost; 1 mark: diversion of resources [2]

items.stem: Extract: Esteria relies on copper for 70% of its exports. Over five years its export price index fell to 82 while its import price index rose to 110. External debt has reached 90% of GDP and the government is negotiating an IMF loan, while a foreign mining company plans a new mine. (a) Explain two conditions the IMF might attach to its loan. (b) Discuss whether the new mine will benefit the country’s development.
items.answer: (a) Fiscal consolidation, removal of subsidies, exchange-rate flexibility, privatisation, anti-corruption measures. (b) Jobs, tax, FDI inflows, technology vs repatriation, environmental damage, deepening commodity dependence; conditions such as royalties and linkages.

items.stem: The terms of trade index is calculated as
options: value of exports − value of imports
index of export prices ÷ index of import prices × 100
index of import prices ÷ index of export prices × 100
items.answer: index of export prices ÷ index of import prices × 100
items.markingKey: A rise is an “improvement” (favourable).

items.stem: Explain why an improvement in the terms of trade may not improve the current account.
items.answer: If export prices rise and demand is price elastic, export volumes fall and revenue may fall; a rise in ToT may reflect a loss of competitiveness.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: price elastic demand; 1 mark: competitiveness [2]

items.stem: Explain two ways a commodity-dependent country could reduce its vulnerability.
items.answer: Diversify into manufacturing/services; add value through processing; stabilisation funds/sovereign wealth funds; hedging; regional trade agreements.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each identified, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: In Marvona, the export price index rises to 110 and the import price index to 125 (base year = 100). Calculate the terms of trade index.

Fendaria earns $30 billion from exports, of which 60% comes from crude oil. Its export price index is 92 and import price index 100. (a) Calculate the terms of trade index and state whether it shows an improvement or deterioration since the base year. (b) If the world price of crude oil then falls by 20% with unchanged volumes, calculate the fall in export earnings. (c) Explain why commodity dependence is a problem.
items.answer: (a) 92: deterioration (b) $3.6 billion (c) Volatile prices make export earnings, government revenue and growth unstable; low income elasticity limits long-run growth; Dutch disease.
items.markingKey: (a) ToT formula and interpretation [2]; (b) share × fall [1]; (c) two developed points [2].

items.stem: Coffee accounts for most of Istrana’s export earnings. (a) Explain what is meant by the terms of trade and how they are measured. (b) Consider whether specialising in primary commodities is the best strategy for low-income countries.
items.answer: (a) Explanation of the theory (with a described diagram where relevant), drawing on: Comparative advantage, export earnings, FDI in extraction. (b) Case for the view: Comparative advantage, export earnings, FDI in extraction. Case against / evaluation: Volatile prices, deteriorating ToT, Dutch disease, low value added; diversification and processing. Conclusion: a judgement on the conditions under which the view holds.
items.markingKey: (a) Knowledge and understanding of the theory, clear analytical chain; diagram described accurately with labelled axes and curves. (b) Analysis of arguments for and against; evaluation reaches a justified conclusion that weighs the conditions under which the claim holds. Top level needs a judgement, not just a summary.

items.stem: The world price of Lunaria’s main export, cocoa, rises by 40%. Explain the effect on its terms of trade and on its economy.
items.answer: Export price index rises, so ToT improve; export earnings and government revenue rise, but the currency may appreciate and other exports become less competitive (Dutch disease); the boom may be temporary.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ToT improve; 1 mark: wider effect [2]

items.stem: In Selmaria, the export price index rises to 85 and the import price index to 115 (base year = 100). Calculate the terms of trade index.
Which is a likely benefit of FDI for a host developing country?
